Beyond stomachs: DNA metabarcoding, scats and other compositional data

Source: vignettes/articles/other-data.Rmd
other-data.Rmd

DietView was written for stomach contents, but what it needs is more general: a taxon name with a quantity, inside a sampling unit, with covariates. The same structure describes diet from DNA metabarcoding of scats or gut contents, pellets and regurgitates, catch composition from a survey haul, or a benthic grab. This article shows how such data come in:

  • dv_spec(weight_type = , unit_label = ) says what the quantity is (prey mass, sequence reads, or relative read abundance) and what one sampling unit is (a stomach, a scat, a sample), so figures and messages say the right thing;
  • dv_resolution() reports the rank at which identification stops, with or without digestion stages;
  • dv_from_wide() reshapes a wide sample-by-taxon table into the long format;
  • dv_parse_lineage() splits the lineage strings that pipelines report into rank columns;
  • dv_prepare(taxonomy = "gbif") resolves prey outside the marine realm against the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy, with the same rules and review log as WoRMS.
library(DietView)

1. A real case: harbour seal scats from the Salish Sea

salish_seal_dna is the public DNA metabarcoding diet of harbour seals of the Salish Sea (Thomas et al. 2022): 4,625 scats from 52 haul-outs, 2012-2018, one row per prey taxon in a scat, with its share of the scat’s prey DNA. Its lineage, resolved once against WoRMS, ships as salish_seal_lineage.

head(salish_seal_dna[, c("sample_id", "site", "year", "season", "prey_label",
                         "reads_16S", "diet_fraction")])
#>   sample_id   site year season             prey_label reads_16S diet_fraction
#> 1  Pv12.001 Fraser 2012 spring      Alosa sapidissima      1376        0.9731
#> 2  Pv12.001 Fraser 2012 spring        Clupea pallasii        23        0.0163
#> 3  Pv12.001 Fraser 2012 spring  Metacarcinus magister        15        0.0106
#> 4  Pv12.002 Fraser 2012 spring        Clupea pallasii       993        0.2859
#> 5  Pv12.002 Fraser 2012 spring Gasterosteus aculeatus      2480        0.7141
#> 6  Pv12.003 Fraser 2012 spring      Alosa sapidissima         1        0.0385

The scat is the sampling unit, so it goes in the stomach role and is named with unit_label. The DNA share is relative read abundance, so it is declared as such rather than as a weight:

spec_seal <- dv_spec(predator = "predator", stomach = "sample_id",
                     prey_name = "prey_label", weight = "diet_fraction",
                     weight_type = "rra", unit_label = "scat",
                     covariates = c("season", "year", "site", "lab"))
seal <- dv_prepare(salish_seal_dna, spec_seal, taxonomy = "table",
                   lineage = salish_seal_lineage, verbose = FALSE)
seal
#> <dietview_prep>
#>   records   : 11641 
#>   scats     : 4625 
#>   predators : 1 
#>   ranks     : kingdom > phylum > class > order > family > genus > species 
#>   covariates: season, year, site, lab 
#>   source    : table

Occurrence and relative read abundance

Two views answer different questions. The share of prey records (with one record per taxon and scat) and the frequency of occurrence say how often a prey is eaten; the mean RRA says how much of the diet it makes up, each scat weighing the same:

tree_seal <- dv_tree(seal)
fam <- dv_rank_table(tree_seal, "Family")
head(fam[order(-fam$pct_w), c("label", "pct_occ", "pct_w")], 6)
#>           label   pct_occ     pct_w
#> 52 Merlucciidae 15.076024 23.549770
#> 49    Clupeidae 16.733958 22.119605
#> 84   Salmonidae 19.826475 16.157408
#> 59 Embiotocidae  5.248690  5.437847
#> 64     Cottidae  6.494287  5.068601
#> 51      Gadidae  7.482175  4.935487
fo <- dv_fo_table(seal, rank = "species")
head(fo[order(-fo$pct_fo), c("taxon", "n_stomachs", "pct_fo")], 6)
#>                      taxon n_stomachs pct_fo
#> 1          Clupea pallasii       1948  42.12
#> 2     Merluccius productus       1755  37.95
#> 3       Porichthys notatus        608  13.15
#> 4 Oncorhynchus tshawytscha        591  12.78
#> 5      Gadus chalcogrammus        578  12.50
#> 6   Cymatogaster aggregata        575  12.43

Pacific herring is found in more scats than Pacific hake, but hake makes up more of the diet when it is eaten: the two currencies rank them differently, which is why DietView keeps both.

dv_sunburst(tree_seal, mode = "weight", title = "Harbour seal, Salish Sea (mean RRA)")
dv_build_html(seal, output = "salish_seal.html", cross = list("season"))

Where identification stops

Metabarcoding resolves most prey to species, but not all: a short marker can fail to separate close relatives, and the authors then report alternatives (“Sebastes flavidus OR Sebastes melanops”). The frozen lineage keeps what the candidates share (here the genus Sebastes), so those records sit in the unidentified share below the genus, exactly as a digested stomach item would. dv_resolution() measures it, here by laboratory:

res <- dv_resolution(seal, by = "lab")
res[, c("lab", "finest_rank", "n_records", "p_records", "p_weight")]
#>     lab finest_rank n_records   p_records    p_weight
#> 1   DFO       Order         3  0.14471780  0.05269395
#> 2   DFO      Family        17  0.82006753  0.58736356
#> 3   DFO       Genus        11  0.53063193  0.44303242
#> 4   DFO     Species      2042 98.50458273 98.91691007
#> 5   UBC       Order         3  0.06133715  0.10503449
#> 6   UBC      Family        53  1.08362298  0.89682217
#> 7   UBC       Genus        19  0.38846862  0.28006135
#> 8   UBC     Species      4816 98.46657125 98.71808199
#> 9  WDFW      Family       105  2.24502886  1.66822718
#> 10 WDFW       Genus        91  1.94569168  1.77833148
#> 11 WDFW     Species      4481 95.80927945 96.55344135

Without a digestion column, this is the identification-resolution diagnostic; with one, dv_digestion_diagnostic() gives the same table by digestion stage.

2. From an ASV table

A typical output of a metabarcoding pipeline is one row per ASV, a taxonomy string, and one column of read counts per sample. Here are six ASVs from four seal scats (made-up numbers, to show the reshaping):

asv <- data.frame(
  asv = paste0("ASV", 1:6),
  taxonomy = c(
    "k__Animalia;p__Chordata;c__Actinopteri;o__Gadiformes;f__Gadidae;g__Gadus;s__morhua",
    "k__Animalia;p__Chordata;c__Actinopteri;o__Gadiformes;f__Gadidae;g__Gadus;s__morhua",
    "k__Animalia;p__Chordata;c__Actinopteri;o__Clupeiformes;f__Clupeidae;g__Clupea;s__harengus",
    "k__Animalia;p__Chordata;c__Actinopteri;o__Pleuronectiformes;f__;g__;s__",
    "k__Animalia;p__Mollusca;c__Cephalopoda;o__Myopsida;f__Loliginidae;g__Loligo;s__Loligo sp.",
    "Unassigned"),
  scat1 = c(5200, 800, 0, 300, 0, 40),
  scat2 = c(0, 0, 6100, 0, 900, 0),
  scat3 = c(1500, 0, 1500, 0, 0, 10),
  scat4 = c(0, 0, 0, 2500, 2500, 0))
meta <- data.frame(sample = paste0("scat", 1:4), predator = "grey seal",
                   season = c("winter", "winter", "summer", "summer"))

Reshape and parse

dv_from_wide() turns it into one row per ASV in a sample, drops the zeros and joins the sample metadata. ASV1 and ASV2 carry the same taxonomy; collapse_by = "taxonomy" sums them, so that a taxon counts once per sample in the shares of records and in %FO:

long <- dv_from_wide(asv, id_cols = c("asv", "taxonomy"), meta = meta,
                     collapse_by = "taxonomy")
long <- dv_parse_lineage(long, "taxonomy")
long[, c("sample", "reads", "order", "genus", "species", "prey_name")]
#>    sample reads             order  genus         species         prey_name
#> 1   scat1  6000        Gadiformes  Gadus    Gadus morhua      Gadus morhua
#> 2   scat1   300 Pleuronectiformes   <NA>            <NA> Pleuronectiformes
#> 3   scat1    40              <NA>   <NA>            <NA>              <NA>
#> 4   scat2  6100      Clupeiformes Clupea Clupea harengus   Clupea harengus
#> 5   scat2   900          Myopsida Loligo            <NA>            Loligo
#> 6   scat3  1500        Gadiformes  Gadus    Gadus morhua      Gadus morhua
#> 7   scat3  1500      Clupeiformes Clupea Clupea harengus   Clupea harengus
#> 8   scat3    10              <NA>   <NA>            <NA>              <NA>
#> 9   scat4  2500 Pleuronectiformes   <NA>            <NA> Pleuronectiformes
#> 10  scat4  2500          Myopsida Loligo            <NA>            Loligo

The empty fields (f__), the placeholder Unassigned and Loligo sp. become NA: these records stay in the tree, as the explicit unidentified category below the deepest rank they reached, exactly as a stomach item identified only to order.

Reads are not biomass

Sequence reads measure DNA, not prey mass: digestion, tissue type and primer bias all distort the link (Deagle et al. 2019). DietView therefore never labels reads as weight. Two summaries are offered:

  • weight_type = "reads": the share of all reads (pooled), which lets the samples with most reads dominate;
  • weight_type = "rra": the relative read abundance. The reads of each sample are divided by its total before summing, so every sample weighs the same and the share at a rank is the mean RRA over samples.

The shares of prey records stay available and, with one record per taxon and sample, are the occurrence-based view; dv_fo_table() gives the classical frequency of occurrence over samples.

spec <- dv_spec(predator = "predator", stomach = "sample",
                prey_name = "prey_name", weight = "reads",
                weight_type = "rra", unit_label = "scat",
                covariates = "season")
prep <- dv_prepare(long, spec, taxonomy = "columns", verbose = FALSE)
tree <- dv_tree(prep)
dv_rank_table(tree, "Order")
#>                label value_item value_occ pct_occ     value_w      pct_w
#> 9       Clupeiformes          1         2      20 1.369767442 34.2441860
#> 10        Gadiformes          1         2      20 1.444711110 36.1177778
#> 11 Pleuronectiformes          1         2      20 0.547318612 13.6829653
#> 12          Myopsida          1         2      20 0.628571429 15.7142857
#> 13                NA          1         2      20 0.009631407  0.2407852
dv_fo_table(prep, rank = "order")
#>    rank             taxon n_stomachs n_total pct_fo
#> 1 order      Clupeiformes          2       4     50
#> 2 order        Gadiformes          2       4     50
#> 3 order          Myopsida          2       4     50
#> 4 order                NA          2       4     50
#> 5 order Pleuronectiformes          2       4     50

pct_w is the mean RRA. Each figure and dashboard labels it as such:

dv_sunburst(tree, mode = "weight", title = "Grey seal scats (RRA)")
dv_build_html(prep, output = "seal_scats.html", cross = list("season"))

3. Which taxonomy?

Three routes, by what the data already carry:

The data carry Use Why
A lineage string from the assignment step dv_parse_lineage() then taxonomy = "columns" Keeps the reference taxonomy the sequences were assigned with (NCBI, SILVA, BOLD), and needs no network.
Prey names, marine prey taxonomy = "worms" WoRMS is the authority for marine taxa.
Prey names, terrestrial or freshwater prey taxonomy = "gbif" The GBIF Backbone covers all kingdoms.

The names produced by dv_parse_lineage() can also be sent to WoRMS or GBIF, to harmonize a metabarcoding data set with stomach data classified there:

prep_gbif <- dv_prepare(long, spec, taxonomy = "gbif", kingdom = "Animalia")
dv_taxonomy_report(prep_gbif)

GBIF matches are logged like WoRMS matches, with two extra review flags: "higherrank" (the name is unknown to GBIF, but a coarser taxon in it is known, so the lineage stops there) and low_confidence. The GBIF Backbone has no class for some groups (ray-finned fishes sit directly under Chordata); the default gaps = "label" fills that rank as "Chordata (no class)" rather than counting the records as unidentified.

4. Other compositional data

Catch composition, plankton or benthos tables often come with samples in rows and taxa in columns. taxa_in = "columns" reads that layout:

haul <- data.frame(haul = c("H1", "H2"), stratum = c("401", "402"),
                   `Gadus morhua` = c(12.4, 0), `Clupea harengus` = c(30.1, 55.0),
                   check.names = FALSE)
catch <- dv_from_wide(haul, taxa_in = "columns", id_cols = c("haul", "stratum"),
                      sample_col = "haul", value_col = "kg")
catch
#>   haul stratum       prey_name   kg
#> 1   H1     401    Gadus morhua 12.4
#> 2   H1     401 Clupea harengus 30.1
#> 3   H2     402 Clupea harengus 55.0

Then declare the haul as the sampling unit (unit_label = "haul"), the stratum as a covariate (with a constant predator column, e.g. the survey), and the weight in kg as a mass. Everything downstream (sunbursts, covariate strata, the dashboard) works unchanged.

5. What does not fit

Stable isotopes and fatty acids do not identify prey: mixing models (MixSIAR, simmr, QFASA) estimate the contributions of a few source groups chosen by the analyst, with posterior uncertainty. A sunburst of posterior means would hide that uncertainty and the shallow, often functional, grouping of the sources. DietView is not meant for those outputs; it can, however, hold the stomach or DNA data from the same predators on one taxonomic backbone, the reference against which isotope-based diets are often compared.

References

Thomas, A. C., Deagle, B., Nordstrom, C., Majewski, S., Nelson, B. W., Acevedo-Gutiérrez, A., Jeffries, S., Moore, J., Louden, A., Allegue, H., Pearson, S., Schmidt, M., & Trites, A. W. (2022). Data on the diets of Salish Sea harbour seals from DNA metabarcoding. Scientific Data, 9, 68. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-022-01152-5

Deagle, B. E., Thomas, A. C., McInnes, J. C., Clarke, L. J., Vesterinen, E. J., Clare, E. L., Kartzinel, T. R., & Eveson, J. P. (2019). Counting with DNA in metabarcoding studies: How should we convert sequence reads to dietary data? Molecular Ecology, 28(2), 391-406.
